prize_parts.citation: for showing how collateral constraints and asset prices amplify and propagate shocks, creating the theory of credit cycles

statement.case_for: My configuration has changed. I now propose a single part, B002, credited to Kiyotaki and Moore, and I have withdrawn the second part (Pakes alone for B012). The test is the one I used in round 1: a clear origin, durable use across fields, and years of confirmation. Kiyotaki-Moore (1997) is a single mechanism with unambiguous two-author credit. Borrowing limits tied to collateral values feed back on asset prices, so small or temporary shocks become large and persistent. The mechanism is now a standard building block in macro-finance and in post-2008 policy modelling, and nearly three decades have passed. Why I dropped the second part: the exchange showed me that crediting Pakes alone costs more than I weighed in round 1. Stromberg, Hjalmarsson and Andersson treat the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes trio as the unit of the demand-estimation breakthrough. If that is right, a Pakes-only citation misdescribes the discovery. I accepted that loss in round 1 only to fit two parts under the three-person cap. That is a poor reason to compromise accurate credit, and the pairing of macro-finance with empirical IO also has no shared theme. The cause is attribution accuracy. It is not that no other member proposed the pairing. Gertler: my round-1 argument that he would take a cap slot no longer applies with one part. I still leave him out, now purely on scope. A three-name citation reads as a claim about financial frictions in general. That makes Gilchrist an obvious omission, ties the credit to the Bernanke lineage, and splits Gertler's credit with B043. I hold this less firmly than before. On the chair's question about adjacency to recent prizes, I treat overlap with 2008, 2022 and 2024 as a timing and balance consideration. It is not a merit criterion, and I would apply it the same way to B002, B025, B050 and B021.
statement.case_against: B002 is the closest call in my ordering, and it competes with B012 in its full trio form. Three reservations stand. First, the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises is adjacent, and the Committee may judge the territory covered. Second, empirical identification of the size of collateral amplification is weaker than the theory's influence. B012 has the stronger record of confirmation and use in applied work, and I count that in its favour. Third, a prize resting on one 1997 paper plus its follow-up is narrower than a framework with many contributors, and leaving out Gertler and Gilchrist may look incomplete to those who see the accelerator as part of the same insight. My tie-break between B002 and B012 is attribution clarity, which is a judgement. Dropping B012 as a preferred part also means the preferred configuration gives no recognition to the BLP estimation breakthrough, which is equally mature.

responses.point: Hassler prefers Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He centres the award on collateral constraints and the wider finding that financial frictions propagate fluctuations. He treats Gertler's intermediary-based work (with Kiyotaki and with Karadi) as separable from the 2022 recognition, and he accepts the two-name version as a fallback.
responses.response: Your point that Gertler's later work connects to the collateral mechanism is fair, and it is the strongest reason for three names. The supplied record lets me separate that work from the 2022 prize by description only, not by evidence, so I cannot settle your question. My round-1 reason for dropping him, the cap slot, no longer applies to a single-part configuration, and I say so plainly. What remains is scope. A three-name citation about financial frictions in propagation is broader than the collateral-and-credit-cycle achievement. It leaves Gilchrist as the obvious omission and splits Gertler's credit with B043. I would not call the three-name version indefensible. If the Committee words it around propagation and keeps the Kiyotaki-Moore core first, I would prefer it to losing that core.

responses.point: Stromberg anchors B012 on the BLP demand-estimation core with Pakes's dynamic-industry work. He argues the three-name cap is a constraint every multi-contributor candidate faces, not a defect of this one, and that three decades of identification and robustness debate without displacement show maturity.
responses.response: This argument changed my configuration. If the BLP trio is the unit, my Pakes-alone second part understated the discovery, and I had accepted that loss in round 1 only because the cap bound a two-part design. I agree the cap is a constraint on every candidate, and that surviving three decades of critique counts as maturity. B012 in its full trio form is now my first alternative. I no longer want a configuration that cuts Berry and Levinsohn to make room for something else.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson describes B012 as both a method and a framework that recovers substitution patterns, markups and welfare. She says the tools-versus-discovery objection is the strongest general one, and that if Bresnahan were equal in kind then no three-person set around BLP would be fully defensible.
responses.response: I agree this is more than technique, and I cannot resolve the Bresnahan question from the supplied evidence. Where I differ is on what separates B002 and B012 for me. B012 has the better record of confirmation and use in applied work, and its structural assumptions have been tested by long critique. B002 has the cleaner origin. I do not think the gap is large, and my ordering rests on attribution clarity, not on a view that mechanisms outrank methods. This is also my answer to the chair's question on mechanism versus method: I would not let either side decide it by category.

responses.point: Krusell narrowed B002 to Kiyotaki and Moore after reading colleagues. He regards the quantitative size of collateral amplification as debated and the overlap with the 2022 prize as a real risk. He also asks that Gertler's credit not be blurred with B043.
responses.response: I agree with your narrowing and with the B043 point. On the chair's evidence question, I would accept evidence that exogenous variation in collateral values moves firm borrowing and investment by magnitudes consistent with the model's amplification, and that demand shifts alone do not explain it. The supplied record contains no such evidence, so I cannot change a ranking on it. I treat identification as a standing discount on B002, comparable to the structural-assumption discount on B012. On the 2022 overlap I am a little less worried than you, since I read that prize as being about banks, runs and intermediation. But it is a judgement for the Committee.

responses.point: Friberg notes that I ranked B025 last of my eight. He argues the 2008 prize recognised scale economies and trade patterns, while Melitz-style selection and reallocation is a distinct mechanism. He would keep Melitz as the core even if Helpman's credit is judged better placed elsewhere.
responses.response: You have moved me on part of this. I weighted the Krugman overlap too heavily at opening: selection and reallocation among firms is a different mechanism from scale economies and variety. I would now place B025 above where I put it in round 1. What still keeps it outside my preferred part and my alternatives is attribution: Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum are not on the ballot, and Helpman's credit is spread across several strands. I agree with Dreber and you that Eaton-Kortum should not be bundled in.

responses.point: Fredriksson prefers B050. He records my past co-authorship disclosure about Torsten Persson and says the Committee should not read my B050 ranking as independent confirmation. He concedes that cross-country constitutional identification is thinner than the theory's influence.
responses.response: The caution is right, but the factual basis was weaker than my round-1 responses implied. My profile lists a co-author named only 'Persson' on a corruption paper and gives no first name. It does not link that person to Torsten Persson, and I repeat that my earlier identification is unverified. B050 leaves my alternatives only because B012 now takes a slot, and my opening ranked B001 above B050. That is not a response to the disclosure. On the merits I accept your distinction that the 2024 institutions prize concerns long-run prosperity while B050 concerns fiscal-policy mechanisms. I still weigh the identification problem you concede, but adjacency to 2024 is not a scientific demerit.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises as covering the collateral-constraint mechanism. I cannot resolve this from the supplied record.
How strongly the evidence supports quantitatively large collateral amplification, which is the main discount on B002 relative to its conceptual standing.
Whether leaving out Gertler (and Gilchrist) makes the B002 citation look incomplete, or whether a three-name version around financial frictions in propagation would be the more accurate credit.

Whether B012 in trio form should outrank B002 on the stronger confirmation record. My tie-break is attribution clarity, and a Committee that weighs measurement and applied reach more heavily could reasonably reverse it.
Whether Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin should change the B012 laureate set. I rely on colleagues' descriptions and have not verified relative credit.
B001 remains an alternative on my opening ranking (third). I did not re-argue it this round, and I am unsure how the Committee would weigh a game-theory threshold against Rubinstein-Wolinsky.
statement.conflict_note: No collaborator among the credited names of B002, B012 or B001 appears in my supplied profile. I share Stockholm University with committee members Hassler, Krusell and Boppart (different departments). All three prefer B002 and none is a candidate, so I do not treat their agreement as independent confirmation of my view. I gave the 2024 presentation speech on institutions and prosperity. The profile notes that such speeches do not establish private preferences, but it bears on how adjacent B050 should be read. My field of comparative political institutions is adjacent to B050, which is no longer among my alternatives. Correction to round 1: my profile lists a co-author named only 'Persson' (corruption as a collective-action problem, with Rothstein) and no first name. It does not link that person to Torsten Persson, so my round-1 statement of past co-authorship with Torsten Persson is unverified and should be given no weight in either direction. I disclose this and do not adjudicate it.
